content: The evidence reviews summarized in Chapter 8 of the WHO Guidelines on Sanitation and Health provide detailed insights into the effectiveness and implementation of various sanitation interventions. 1. Effectiveness of Sanitation Interventions in Achieving and Sustaining Access, Uptake, and Use of Sanitation Studies reviewed spanned from 1950 to December 31, 2015, with no language or geographic restrictions. A total of 37 household studies were included, comprising 10 randomized controlled trials (RCTs), 1 non-RCT, 6 controlled before-and-after (CBA) studies, 11 uncontrolled before-and-after studies, and 9 non-randomized control trials. Four school-based studies were also included, with 1 RCT and 3 non-RCTs. The Liverpool Quality Appraisal Tool (LQAT) was adapted for quantitative intervention studies, and most studies indicated some risk of bias. The quality of evidence was rated as Low to Very Low using the GRADE framework. 2. Effectiveness of Sanitation Interventions in Reducing Environmental Faecal Load A literature review focused on leakage along the sanitation service chain for pit latrines, septic systems, and sewerage. Searches were conducted in Web of Science and Google Scholar between March 15, 2015, and April 24, 2015. No specific geographic or economic restrictions were applied. The quality of evidence was assessed using an adapted LQAT, with an average bias score of 8/12, indicating a relatively high risk of bias. The GRADE assessment rated the evidence as Low or Very Low. 3. Effectiveness of Sanitation Interventions in Reducing Exposure to Faecal Pathogens Studies reviewed spanned from 1950 to December 2015, with no language or geographic restrictions. A total of 23 studies on faecal-oral transmission were included, comprising 8 RCTs, 1 non-RCT, 1 quasi-RCT, 11 cross-sectional studies, 1 case-control study, and 1 cohort study. Six studies focused on water supply distance, all of which were cross-sectional. Urban and rural settings were represented, with 10 urban, 15 rural, and 3 mixed studies. The quality of evidence was rated as Low or Very Low using the GRADE framework. 4. Effectiveness of Sanitation Interventions in Improving Health Outcomes (Infectious Diseases, Nutritional Status, Well-being, and Educational Outcomes) This review was based on original studies, including RCTs, quasi-RCTs, non-RCTs, CBAs, interrupted time-series studies, cohort studies, and cross-sectional studies. The evidence was assessed using an abridged LQAT for experimental studies. The GRADE framework was used to update a diarrhoea review by Pruss-Ustun et al. (2014), with 65 studies included, 40 of which were used in meta-analyses. Evidence quality varied by helminth species: Ascaris lumbricoides: 39 studies (5 RCTs, 4 non-RCTs, 27 cross-sectional, 1 CBA, 1 case series, 1 mixed methods). Evidence quality: Very Low. Trichuris trichiura: 34 studies (4 RCTs, 3 non-RCTs, 24 cross-sectional, 1 CBA, 1 mixed methods). Evidence quality: Very Low. Hookworm: 42 studies (4 RCTs, 2 non-RCTs, 30 cross-sectional, 2 CBAs, 1 case series, 1 mixed methods). Evidence quality: Low. Strongyloides stercoralis: 9 studies (1 non-RCT, 7 cross-sectional, 1 cohort). Evidence quality: Not assessed. 5. Effectiveness of Sanitation Interventions in Preventing Trachoma An updated review by Stocks et al. (2014) included 46 studies, all used in meta-analyses. Active trachoma: 41 studies (3 RCTs, 34 cross-sectional, 3 case-control, 1 case series). Evidence quality: High. Chlamydia trachomatis: 10 studies (2 RCTs, 8 cross-sectional). Evidence quality: Moderate. 6. Effectiveness of Sanitation Interventions in Preventing Schistosomiasis An updated review by Grimes et al. (2014) included 30 studies, 23 of which were used in meta-analyses. Schistosoma mansoni: 23 studies (22 cross-sectional, 1 case-control). Evidence quality: Not scored due to lack of intervention studies. Schistosoma haematobium: 10 studies (9 cross-sectional, 1 case-control). Evidence quality: Not scored due to lack of intervention studies. 7. Effectiveness of Sanitation Interventions in Improving Nutritional Outcomes An updated review by Dangour et al. (2013) included 17 studies, 9 of which were used in meta-analyses. Weight-for-age and underweight: 14 studies (7 RCTs, 6 non-RCTs, 1 quasi-RCT). Evidence quality: Low. Weight-for-height and wasting: 7 studies (4 RCTs, 3 non-RCTs). Evidence quality: Low. Height-for-age and stunting: 14 studies (8 RCTs, 6 non-RCTs). Evidence quality: Very Low. 8. Impact of WASH Interventions on People Living with HIV A systematic review focused on resource-limited countries included 4 sanitation studies (1 RCT, 2 cross-sectional, 1 case-control). Evidence quality was categorized as Strong, Medium, or Weak based on study design, cohort population, and sample size. 9. Influence of Policies and Governance on Sanitation Access and Uptake A review of 68 studies (6 qualitative, 25 quantitative, 9 mixed methods, 28 case studies) assessed the role of policies, regulations, and governance in sanitation adoption. Evidence quality was assessed using LQAT and categorized as Strong, Moderate, or Weak. These findings highlight the variability in evidence quality across different sanitation interventions and outcomes, emphasizing the need for rigorous study designs and comprehensive assessments to inform public health policies.
